summary.text: 20-year-old male with schizophrenia who received Invega Sustenna (paliperidone) loading doses (234 mg and 156 mg) during a 3-week psychiatric admission elsewhere and, per his mother, had been acting this way since discharge 1 day earlier; he was brought to the emergency room with erratic behavior, verbal and motor hypoactivity, sialorrhea, generalized stiffness and slowed speech.

In the ED he received IM benztropine 1 mg and IM lorazepam 2 mg with partial resolution. Consultation-Liaison psychiatry found catatonia with arm posturing and a Bush-Francis score of 15; it mildly improved (BFCRS 12) over a 2-day medical stay. On Day 3 in inpatient psychiatry he still had stiffness, posturing, slowed speech, disorganized thought with grandiosity and auditory hallucinations.

He was started on oral risperidone 1 mg twice daily, benztropine 1 mg twice daily, valproate 500 mg twice daily and oral lorazepam 1 mg twice daily, improved significantly (normal ambulation, no stiffness, regular speech, hallucinations abated, some residual grandiosity), had lorazepam tapered off by 10 days, and was discharged with oral medications and outpatient follow-up.

summary.text: 24-year-old African American female with schizophrenia admitted to a psychiatric hospital after being found at a train station with disorganized behavior and auditory hallucinations, with poor oral intake and difficulty swallowing prompting transfer to the medical unit.

Psychiatric assessment showed stiffness, slow movement, unsteadiness, difficulty eating and drinking and a Bush-Francis score of 11 consistent with catatonia; she had received Invega Sustenna 234 mg then 156 mg IM 6 weeks before admission with no catatonic symptoms before the injectable; abdominal imaging for ovarian teratomas was negative and autoimmune encephalitis was excluded.

Oral paliperidone was stopped and risperidone (1 mg then 2 mg BID), lorazepam, sertraline and benztropine were given; after 3 weeks motor symptoms near-totally resolved and lorazepam was stopped, risperidone Consta 25 mg IM was given before discharge, and at six months she continued outpatient follow-up with no reported side effects.

article_limitations: Two-patient case series (Case 1 and Case 2) plus a literature review: Table 1 rows (Johnson et al., Tu et al., Coffey, McKeown et al., Xiong et al., Mall et al.) and discussion statements describe published cases or general knowledge and are not extracted as facts of the index patients.

The introduction states BFCRS scores of 15 and 11 and "moderate to severe catatonia" for the two patients together; per-patient BFCRS scores are taken from the case sections and no per-patient severity grade is assigned.
Catatonia is attributed to paliperidone by the authors; no causality scale is reported.
No laboratory values, vital signs or imaging details beyond a negative abdominal imaging result (Case 2) are reported; the article has no figures or supplements.

Case 1: "originally from Jamaica" is kept in the case description only (no demographic field for national origin); the individual dates and order of the 234 mg and 156 mg loading doses are not given for either case.

Case 1 loading-dose timing differs between b00006 ('loading doses on the day of discharge') and b00008 (series during the prior admission, last dose the day before the current admission); kept as an ambiguity with the broader admission time.
Presenting-finding times are taken only from each finding's own sentence (ED presentation for Case 1; 'On psychiatric assessment' only for the Case 2 findings in that sentence).
